concepts.topicTitle: Essence of Entrepreneurship and Societal Value Creation
concepts.label: Entrepreneurship: Turning Ideas into Ventures
concepts.cardText: Running a lemonade stall at a school festival shows the essence of running a business: planning, organising and learning by doing. You decide how much to spend on lemons and sugar, how much to charge a glass, and whether you made a profit or a loss. This is entrepreneurship, a process through which individuals, or a group of individuals, convert a potential idea into a business venture. Entrepreneurs are curious individuals who see opportunities where others see challenges and turn that spark into action, driven by passion and a commitment to creating value for society. Their tasks are to identify a problem and solve it with an innovative solution, combine various factors of production, take risks by investing money and time, make key decisions on how the business operates, and contribute to the welfare of society. The Jataka tale of the young man who turned a dead mouse into a fortune shows that hard work and a clever mind can start something big.

concepts.topicTitle: Essence of Entrepreneurship and Societal Value Creation
concepts.label: Entrepreneurs in Action: Lijjat Papad and Mohan Singh Oberoi
concepts.cardText: In 1959 seven ordinary homemakers from a Mumbai chawl gathered on a rooftop with borrowed equipment, a recipe and ₹80, aiming to earn extra income by making papads. They had no degrees, investors or master plan, but they had grit and unity: each woman took dough home, rolled papads and returned them with the condition that the quality had to be consistent. They formed a cooperative society where every member is an equal owner and profits are shared equally, registered in 1962 as Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad. By 2023 it had over 45,000 women members, 83 branches and a turnover of ₹1,600 crore, and it helped thousands of women become financially independent. Mohan Singh Oberoi, born in 1898, started as a hotel desk clerk earning ₹50 a month, learned every aspect of hotel operations and in 1934 mortgaged his wife's jewellery and invested all his savings to buy a small hotel. He built one of India's largest hotel chains and received the Padma Bhushan in 2001. His journey shows that entrepreneurship is not only about a good idea: it involves planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management of different areas of the business.

concepts.topicTitle: The Business Plan as a Strategic Roadmap
concepts.label: What a Business Plan Is and Why It Matters
concepts.cardText: If you and your friends decide to open a bakery, you must consider many crucial questions, identify challenges and plan at every stage before starting; this is when a business plan is developed. A business plan is a written document, a blueprint explaining the goals of the business and the steps to achieve them. It guides the entrepreneur from the initial idea stage to starting and running the business, and serves as a roadmap for decision making, helping them stay organised, set priorities and work systematically to grow the business. Two early questions come from understanding the market. Needs and idea: to know what people want you must understand customer needs, such as whether they prefer fresh bread, cakes, pastries or healthier whole wheat options. Potential customers: knowing your customers helps decide what products to offer, such as cupcakes for children or savoury snacks for young adults. Money and costs: a robust financial start means planning finances and estimating the initial investment, including equipment, rent, salaries, ingredients and packaging, and deciding how to arrange funds through savings, bank loans, friends, relatives or investors.

concepts.topicTitle: The Business Plan as a Strategic Roadmap
concepts.label: Practical Choices in a Business Plan: Place, People, Price, Promotion and Risk
concepts.cardText: The rest of a business plan covers where, who, how much, how to reach customers and what could go wrong. Location: choose the right place, perhaps a busy area near schools, colleges or markets, or sell online or through mobile apps to reach more people. Human resources: decide how many people to hire and train and the skills needed, such as bakers, helpers and staff for billing or delivery. Pricing and profits: fix prices carefully so that they cover costs and generate profit but also remain affordable, perhaps with a range of options such as cheaper mini cake jars. Promotion or marketing: spread awareness through social media, posters and special offers, and think about packaging and customer service. Challenges and risks: threats that disrupt operations or cause losses, such as high competition, rising raw material costs, changing customer preferences and volatile cash flows, which are an inevitable part of every business venture.

concepts.topicTitle: Functional Areas of a Business and Financial Performance
concepts.label: The Four Functional Areas of a Business
concepts.cardText: Departments or groups within a company that focus on distinct tasks and shared skills are known as functional areas. The questions in a business plan can be grouped into four main functional areas: management and operations, finance and accounting, human resources, and marketing and sales. Each has a specific function and helps the business run smoothly; they improve decision making and ensure resources are used properly, and together they provide structure and better coordination so the business can grow. Management involves planning, organising and guiding the use of resources to achieve business goals, while operations focuses on producing and delivering goods or services efficiently and on time. Human resources are the individuals employed by the entrepreneur, and this area hires and trains staff and creates a motivating workplace, since people are the heart of every business. The marketing and sales team attracts customers and convinces them to buy, through a catchy name, social media and discounts. Finance and accounting is the fourth, managing money wisely.

concepts.topicTitle: Functional Areas of a Business and Financial Performance
concepts.label: Finance, Accounting and the Profit and Loss Account
concepts.cardText: Finance is the management of money in a business: planning, obtaining and using funds to help the business operate and grow. For a bakery this means paying fixed costs such as rent and equipment, paying variable costs such as ingredients, salaries and packaging, investing in growth, and managing profits and cash flow. Accounting is the process of recording, organising and reporting a business's financial transactions, keeping track of money coming in (revenue) and money going out (expenses). A fixed cost remains constant regardless of production or sales, while a variable cost changes in direct proportion to the volume produced or sold. One important record is the profit and loss account (income statement), which shows whether the business made a profit or a loss over a period such as a month or a year. Profit = Total Revenue – Total Expenses. In the sample ABC bakery account, total income of ₹2,95,000 less total expenses of ₹2,22,000 gives a profit before tax of ₹73,000, and after tax of ₹13,000 a profit after tax of ₹60,000.

concepts.topicTitle: Traditional Communities, Innovation, and the Modern Startup Ecosystem
concepts.label: India's Traditional Entrepreneurial Communities: The Chettiars
concepts.cardText: Entrepreneurship in India has deep roots among traditional communities, where skills, occupations and occupational knowledge have been passed down through generations. Long before modern startups, these communities practised self-employment, innovation and trade, forming the backbone of India's local economy. The Chettiar (Nattukottai Chettiar) community from Tamil Nadu is a well-known example. Historically, Chettiars were traders, bankers and moneylenders, operating across India and in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia. They were known for strong business ethics and trust-based lending, excellent accounting and record-keeping skills, and reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education and community welfare. They built wealth through trade in salt, rice, textiles and finance, often without formal banks, and even today their example shows how risk-taking, discipline and long-term vision can build sustainable businesses rooted in tradition.

concepts.topicTitle: Traditional Communities, Innovation, and the Modern Startup Ecosystem
concepts.label: Startups and Their Contribution to the Nation
concepts.cardText: India's vibrant startup ecosystem is built not only on innovation but also on perseverance. A startup is a young, early-stage company founded by entrepreneurs offering an innovative product or service. All entrepreneurs should be aware that a business may end in failure; some startups grow rapidly while others struggle or close, but there is nothing wrong with failure if an honest effort has been made, because every unsuccessful attempt offers lessons for stronger ideas later. Today India is the third-largest startup ecosystem in the world, powered by its young and talented population, with around 120 unicorns in 2025 in areas such as e-commerce, fin-tech, health-tech and agri-tech, and hubs in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai and Delhi NCR. These ventures create jobs, support sustainability and drive growth. The government supports them through schemes such as Startup India, in line with Atmanirbhar Bharat, and entrepreneurship will play a vital role in the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Businesses also contribute by producing goods and services, creating jobs and income, paying taxes, making innovations, improving quality of life and practising corporate social responsibility.
